q: The nucleus of an atom is made up of:
x: In the simple model of the atom, protons and neutrons (together called nucleons) form the nucleus, while electrons move around it outside the nucleus.

q: The atomic number Z of an element is the number of:
o: Protons plus electrons in its atom
x: Z is the number of protons (the charge number) of the nucleus. The total number of protons and neutrons is the mass number A.

q: How many neutrons are there in a nucleus of ²³⁸₉₂U?
x: Number of neutrons N = A − Z = 238 − 92 = 146. 238 is the total number of nucleons and 92 the number of protons.

q: Isotopes of an element have:
o: The same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
The same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
The same mass number but different atomic numbers
Different numbers of protons and electrons
x: Isotopes have the same atomic number Z (same element) but different numbers of neutrons, so their mass numbers differ. Nuclei with the same A but different Z are isobars.

q: Which pair of nuclei are isotopes of the same element?
x: ¹²₆C and ¹⁴₆C both have Z = 6 but 6 and 8 neutrons. ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N have the same mass number but are different elements.

q: A neutral atom of ³⁵₁₇Cl contains:
x: Z = 17 protons; N = 35 − 17 = 18 neutrons; a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, 17.

q: Different isotopes of the same element have the same chemical properties because they have the same:
x: Chemical behaviour depends on the electrons. Isotopes have the same number of protons and so, as neutral atoms, the same number of electrons; only the neutron number and mass differ.

q: Tritium, ³₁H, is an isotope of hydrogen. Its nucleus contains:
x: Z = 1 gives 1 proton and A = 3 gives 3 nucleons, so there are 2 neutrons. Deuterium (²₁H) has 1 proton and 1 neutron.

q: A nucleus has mass number 56 and contains 30 neutrons. How many electrons are there in a neutral atom of this element?
x: Z = A − N = 56 − 30 = 26 protons, and a neutral atom has the same number of electrons, 26. Using the neutron number gives 30 by mistake.

q: Which statement about the simple nuclear model of the atom is correct?
o: The electrons make up most of the mass of the atom
The nucleus fills most of the volume of the atom
Neutrons move in orbits around the nucleus
Almost all the mass is in a tiny positively charged nucleus, with electrons outside it
x: The nucleus is extremely small compared with the atom but holds nearly all its mass and all its positive charge. Electrons, of very small mass, occupy the space around it.

q: An alpha particle is identical to:
x: An alpha particle consists of 2 protons and 2 neutrons, i.e. a helium nucleus ⁴₂He, with charge +2e.

q: Radium-226 (²²⁶₈₈Ra) decays by emitting an alpha particle. The daughter nucleus is:
x: Alpha emission lowers A by 4 and Z by 2: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He.

q: When a nucleus emits a beta particle (an electron), its mass number and atomic number change as follows:
o: A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2
A is unchanged and Z falls by 1
A is unchanged and Z rises by 1
A rises by 1 and Z is unchanged
x: In beta-minus decay a neutron in the nucleus changes into a proton and an electron, and the electron is emitted. The nucleon number stays the same and Z increases by 1, e.g. ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N.

q: When a nucleus emits gamma radiation:
o: Neither its mass number nor its atomic number changes
x: Gamma rays are high-energy photons with no charge and no mass, so emitting them only lowers the energy of the nucleus; A and Z stay the same.

q: Which list puts the three radiations in order of DECREASING penetrating power?
x: Gamma rays are the most penetrating (need thick lead), beta particles are stopped by a few mm of aluminium, and alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper. The ionising order is the reverse.

q: A beam containing alpha, beta and gamma radiation passes through an electric field. Which radiation passes through undeflected?
x: Gamma rays are uncharged electromagnetic waves, so electric and magnetic fields do not deflect them. Alpha (positive) and beta (negative) particles are deflected in opposite directions.

q: Radioactive decay is described as random. This means that:
o: The total number of decays per second can never be estimated
It is impossible to predict which nucleus will decay next or exactly when
Each nucleus decays after the same fixed time
The nuclei decay one after another in a fixed order
x: Each nucleus has a certain chance of decaying in a given time, but we cannot say which one will decay or when. For a large number of nuclei the average rate can still be predicted, which is why half-life is useful.

q: Radioactive decay is called spontaneous because its rate:
o: Is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical combination
Increases when the sample is heated
Can be stopped by putting the sample under high pressure
Changes when the element forms a chemical compound
x: Decay happens on its own inside the nucleus and cannot be speeded up or slowed down by physical or chemical conditions such as temperature, pressure or chemical bonding.

q: A nucleus of ²³⁸₉₂U emits one alpha particle and then two beta particles (electrons). The final nucleus is:
x: Alpha: A = 238 − 4 = 234, Z = 92 − 2 = 90. Two beta decays: A stays 234, Z = 90 + 2 = 92. The result ²³⁴₉₂U is an isotope of the original element.

q: Thorium-232 (²³²₉₀Th) decays through a series of alpha and beta (electron) emissions to lead-208 (²⁰⁸₈₂Pb). How many alpha and beta particles are emitted?
x: A falls by 24, so 24/4 = 6 alpha decays, which lower Z by 12 to 78. Z must end at 82, so 4 beta decays each raise Z by 1.

q: The half-life of a radioactive element is the time taken for:
o: Half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay
All the nuclei in a sample to decay
The mass number of each nucleus to halve
The sample to lose half of its electrons
x: Half-life T½ is the time in which half of the undecayed nuclei present decay, so the number of undecayed nuclei (and the activity) falls to half.

q: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 3 days. What fraction of the original undecayed nuclei is left after 9 days?
x: 9 days is 3 half-lives, so the fraction left is (½)³ = 1/8. 1/3 comes from dividing 9 by 3 without halving.

q: A sample contains 64 mg of a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 2 hours. How much of the isotope remains undecayed after 8 hours?
x: 8 hours = 4 half-lives: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 mg. 16 mg is what remains after only 2 half-lives.

q: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 693 s. Using λ = 0.693/T½, its decay constant is:
x: λ = 0.693/693 = 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Inverting the formula by mistake gives 10³ s⁻¹.

q: The decay constant of a radioactive isotope is 0.0693 per day. Its half-life is:
x: T½ = 0.693/λ = 0.693/0.0693 = 10 days. Multiplying instead of dividing would give a tiny value, about 0.05 day.

q: The SI unit of the decay constant λ is:
x: λ = 0.693/T½, and 0.693 has no unit, so λ has the unit of 1/time, s⁻¹. It is the fraction of nuclei decaying per second.

q: The activity of a radioactive sample is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei. After two half-lives the activity becomes:
x: Activity = λN. After two half-lives N is (½)² = ¼ of its starting value, so the activity is also one-quarter.

q: The count rate from a radioactive sample falls from 1600 counts per minute to 100 counts per minute in 20 minutes (background ignored). The half-life is:
In 40 days, 15/16 of the nuclei in a radioactive sample decay. The half-life of the isotope is:
x: If 15/16 have decayed, 1/16 = (½)⁴ remain, so 4 half-lives have passed: T½ = 40/4 = 10 days.

q: The initial mass of a radioactive sample is doubled. Its half-life:
x: Half-life depends only on the isotope (T½ = 0.693/λ), not on how much of it there is. A bigger sample has more decays per second but the same half-life.

q: Nuclear radiation damages living cells mainly because it:
o: Heats the cells until they boil
Ionises atoms and molecules in the cells, such as DNA
Adds extra protons to the cell nuclei
x: Alpha, beta and gamma radiation knock electrons out of atoms. This ionisation breaks molecules such as DNA, which can kill cells or make them grow abnormally.

q: A radioactive source widely used in radiotherapy to destroy cancer cells with gamma rays is:
x: Cobalt-60 emits strong gamma rays and is used to irradiate tumours. Carbon-14 is used in dating, and sodium-24 as a tracer for blood flow.

q: To check how well a patient's thyroid gland is working, a doctor gives a small amount of a radioactive tracer. A suitable tracer is:
x: The thyroid takes up iodine, so radioactive iodine-131 collects there and its radiation can be detected from outside to show how the gland is working.

q: Gamma rays are used to sterilise sealed packs of syringes and surgical instruments because they:
o: Make the instruments radioactive, which kills germs later
Are stopped by the packaging, which keeps germs out
Penetrate the packaging and kill bacteria without heating the contents
Change the metal of the instruments into a germ-free isotope
x: Gamma rays pass through the sealed plastic and kill microorganisms. Items can be sterilised after packing and without heat, and they do not become radioactive.

q: The SI unit of absorbed dose, equal to 1 joule of radiation energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue, is the:
x: Absorbed dose is measured in gray: 1 Gy = 1 J kg⁻¹. The becquerel and curie are units of activity; the sievert is used for equivalent dose, which also allows for the type of radiation.

q: Damage caused by radiation to the reproductive cells of a person, which may appear in that person's children, is called a:
x: Genetic effects come from damage to the DNA of reproductive cells and can be passed to offspring. Somatic effects, such as burns or cancer, appear in the exposed person.

q: An alpha source outside the body is fairly harmless, but the same source is very dangerous if swallowed or breathed in. This is because alpha particles:
o: Are uncharged and pass straight through the body
Become gamma rays inside the body
Are stopped by skin outside, but inside they ionise nearby cells very strongly
Have a longer half-life inside the body
x: Alpha particles are stopped by the dead outer layer of skin, so an outside source does little harm. Inside the body they give all their energy to nearby tissue, and they are the most strongly ionising radiation.

q: A radioactive tracer is injected into a patient so that an organ can be imaged by a detector outside the body. The tracer should emit:
o: Alpha particles and have a long half-life
Beta particles and have a very long half-life
Alpha particles and have a short half-life
Gamma rays and have a short half-life
x: Gamma rays pass out of the body to reach the detector, whereas alpha and beta particles would be absorbed and harm tissue. A short half-life (hours) gives enough time to image while keeping the patient's dose low.

q: Which of the following would NOT reduce the radiation dose received by a hospital worker handling a gamma source?
o: Keeping a greater distance from the source
Handling the source with long tongs
Spending longer near the source to work more carefully
x: Dose increases with the time spent near a source. Distance (including long tongs) and lead shielding both reduce the dose.
